title: The broken mug reply
scenario:
Leo sells handmade mugs online. A customer, Grace, writes that her mug arrived broken. Leo's rule is simple: he sends a new mug for free and does not give money back. He wants a chat app to help him write a kind, short reply.

He has never used a chat app before. He asks you to help him through the chat.

questions.prompt: Which first message gives Leo the best start?

options.explanation: These are search words. The app must guess the tone, the length and Leo's rule, so it may promise the wrong thing.

options.text: "Write the best possible customer service reply that has ever been written."
options.explanation: It sounds strong, but it gives no facts. The app doesn't know the customer, the problem or Leo's rule.

options.text: "Reply to Grace: her mug arrived broken, I'll send a new one free, no refund. Kind, 4 lines."
options.explanation: Right. It says what Leo wants, the details the app can't guess (name, problem, rule) and the shape (kind, 4 lines). The ChatGPT docs ask for exactly this: the goal, the details that change the answer, and the format.

options.text: "You are a world expert in ceramics, shipping and customer care. Help me with my shop."
options.explanation: A big title does not replace the facts. The app still doesn't know what happened or what Leo will offer.

questions.prompt: The reply looks great, but it promises Grace "a full refund and a 20% discount code". Leo never said that. What should he do?

options.text: Send it as it is, because the app writes customer emails better than he does.
options.explanation: The app invented an offer. If Leo sends it, Grace will expect money back that he doesn't give.

options.text: Tell the app in the same chat to remove the refund and the code, then check again.
options.explanation: Right. Read the answer as a draft and check every claim against the facts. A short follow-up fixes it. The Claude Help Center warns that answers can "look correct but are very mistaken".

options.text: Stop using the app, because a tool that invents an offer can never be trusted.
options.explanation: Every vendor says answers can be wrong. That is why you read and check them, not a reason to give up after one mistake.

options.text: Delete the chat and type exactly the same first message again in a new chat.
options.explanation: The same message can give the same mistake. One short follow-up in this chat is faster and fixes it.

questions.prompt: The next reply is correct, but it is 12 lines long and sounds very formal. What is the best next step?

options.text: Follow up in the same chat: "Make it 4 lines and warmer, and keep the free new mug."
options.explanation: Right. Your first message is only a starting point. A short follow-up that says what to change, and what to keep, fixes it fast.

options.text: Write a new first message of 20 lines with every detail he can think of.
options.explanation: The facts are already right. Only the length and tone are wrong, so a short note is enough.

options.text: Accept it, because a longer and more formal reply always looks more professional.
options.explanation: Leo asked for a kind, short reply. Length and tone are part of the task, so fix them.

options.text: Shorten it by hand and never ask the app for changes, since it got the length wrong.
options.explanation: He can edit by hand, but a follow-up is quicker. Asking for changes is a normal part of a chat.

questions.prompt: Leo keeps using chat apps for his shop: product texts, prices and customer replies. Which moment is the best reason to start a new chat instead of a follow-up?

options.text: The reply is right, but it is a little too formal for his shop.
options.explanation: Tone is a small change. A short follow-up in the same chat fixes it.

options.text: The first reply has one wrong price, and the rest of it is fine.
options.explanation: One wrong fact in a fresh chat is a job for a follow-up: give the app the right price and check again.

options.text: A long, mixed chat keeps bringing back a name he already fixed.
options.explanation: Right. The chat is the app's working memory. When it is long and mixed, and old details keep coming back, a new chat with a short summary of the true facts works better. The Claude Help Center also says you can start a new conversation when you hit the length limit.

options.text: He likes the reply and wants one more version to compare it with.
options.explanation: He can ask for another version in the same chat. Nothing has gone wrong, so there is no need to start again.
